title: The crucifixion as the prophets wrote it — Psalm 22, Isaiah 53, Zechariah 12 and 13, Amos 8, Psalm 69, each in its own words
summary:
It ain't new. Matthew tells the afternoon plainly and keeps pointing at the older scriptures, and the scriptures were already there in detail. The garments:

*And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots.* (Matthew 27:35)

*They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.* (Psalm 22:18)

The mockery, down to the shaking heads and the taunt about trusting:

*And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads,* (Matthew 27:39)

*All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,* (Psalm 22:7)

*He trusted in Elohim (God); let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of Elohim (God).* (Matthew 27:43)

*He trusted on Yahuah (LORD) that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him.* (Psalm 22:8)

The hands and feet:

*For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.* (Psalm 22:16)

The vinegar:

*And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink.* (Matthew 27:48)

*They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.* (Psalm 69:21)

The darkness at noon, which Amos had set in the day of Yahuah (the LORD):

*Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.* (Matthew 27:45)

*And it shall come to pass in that day, saith Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD), that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day:* (Amos 8:9)

Isaiah had written the man himself, despised, silent, wounded for others, buried among the rich:

*He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.* (Isaiah 53:3)

*But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.* (Isaiah 53:5)

*He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.* (Isaiah 53:7)

*And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.* (Isaiah 53:9)

Zechariah had written the sword against the shepherd and the scattering of the sheep, and who it is that was pierced:

*Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith Yahuah Tseva'ot (LORD of hosts): smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones.* (Zechariah 13:7)

*And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.* (Zechariah 12:10)

Mark the speaker in Zechariah. Yahuah (the LORD) says *they shall look upon me whom they have pierced*, and then *they shall mourn for him*. The pierced one is Yahuah (the LORD) in the flesh, and he has a Father; both stand in one verse. The crown of thorns sits beside the oldest curse in the book, read line on line and not as a stated fulfilment:

*And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Yahudim (Jews)!* (Matthew 27:29)

*Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;* (Genesis 3:18)

And the body taken down before night was the Torah kept at the cross:

*His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of Elohim (God);) that thy land be not defiled, which Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) giveth thee for an inheritance.* (Deuteronomy 21:23)

Nothing that afternoon was new. Psalm, prophet and Torah had each written their part of it, and Matthew lets the reader see them come together.

3095.prose: At the place of the skull the soldiers sit down and divide his clothes by lot, and Matthew says plainly that a prophet had said it first. Psalm 22 has the same men, the same garments and the same lots, written long before anyone stood at Golgotha. The afternoon was not made up as it went.
3095.phrase: which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them
3095.sentence: Matthew names the prophet who had already written the dividing of his clothes at the cross.

3096.prose: The people walking past shake their heads at the man on the cross. Psalm 22 already drew that crowd: onlookers who laugh, curl the lip and shake the head. Matthew only reports what happened on the hill, and the psalm had set it down in advance.
3096.phrase: And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads
3096.sentence: The shaking heads of the passing crowd are the ones Psalm 22 drew before the cross stood.

3097.prose: The taunt throws his trust back in his face: let Elohim (God) rescue him now. Psalm 22 puts nearly the same sneer in the mouths of the onlookers, about trusting Yahuah (LORD) and being delivered. At the skull hill the crowd says out loud what the psalm said they would say.
3097.phrase: let him deliver him now, if he will have him
3097.sentence: The mockers at the cross speak the very taunt about trust and rescue that the psalm gave them.

3098.prose: Noon turns to night over the whole land. Amos wrote that day long before: the sun going down at midday and the earth dark in clear light. The dark hours at Golgotha are not a stray wonder. They are the darkness the prophet said would come with that day.
3098.phrase: there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour
3098.sentence: The darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth is the noon darkness Amos set in that day.

3099.prose: Out of the darkness he cries the opening line of Psalm 22, in the speech of the place. The whole psalm stands behind the afternoon: the garments, the mockers, the pierced hands and feet. His cry names the psalm, and the rest of it is being read out in front of the crowd.
3099.phrase: My Elohim (God), my Elohim (God), why hast thou forsaken me?
3099.sentence: His cry from the cross is the first line of Psalm 22, calling the whole psalm to the hill.

3100.prose: A sponge of vinegar is lifted to his mouth on a reed. Psalm 69 has a thirsty man given vinegar to drink, and gall with his food. Matthew has just told of the gall and vinegar at this same hill, so the drink offered now is the one the psalm said he would be handed.
3100.phrase: filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink
3100.sentence: The sponge of vinegar on a reed is the drink that Psalm 69 said would meet his thirst.

3103.prose: Psalm 22 gives what the body went through: poured out like water, bones pulled apart, the heart melted like wax. Matthew gives only the place and the skull. Set side by side, the psalm reads like a man describing from the inside what hanging on that hill did to him.
3103.phrase: all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax
3103.sentence: The poured out water, loosened bones and melted heart tell what the cross did to the body.

3104.prose: A place of a skull, and the psalm already has the dogs closing in around him and his hands and feet pierced. Matthew tells that they crucified him but does not describe the nailing. The psalm does, in one short line, written long before Golgotha had that name.
3104.phrase: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet
3104.sentence: The psalm names the pierced hands and feet that Matthew leaves unspoken on the hill.

3106.prose: The same psalm that opens in abandonment turns here to praise. The sufferer will tell the name to his brothers and sing in the midst of the congregation. The cry at the skull hill is the psalm's first line, and the psalm does not stop there. It ends with a gathered people.
3106.phrase: I will declare thy name unto my brethren
3106.sentence: The psalm moves from the cry on the hill to the name declared among his brothers.

3107.prose: Isaiah wrote the man before he came to the hill: despised, turned away from, a man who knew sorrow well. At Golgotha the whole crowd does exactly that. He is mocked, passed by and left alone, and the faces that turn from him are the ones the prophet described.
3107.phrase: a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief
3107.sentence: Isaiah's despised man of sorrows is the one hanging at the place of the skull.

3108.prose: He is wounded and bruised on the hill, and Isaiah says whose wrongs those wounds answered: ours, not his own. Matthew shows the wounding. Isaiah tells what it was for, and says that by the stripes there is healing for those who had gone astray.
3108.phrase: he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities
3108.sentence: Isaiah says the wounds were taken for other people's wrongs, and healing comes through them.

3109.prose: Through the beating and the taunting the man on the cross answers none of it. Isaiah had already drawn that silence: a lamb led to be killed and a sheep quiet before those who shear it. Golgotha is the place where that silence is kept to the end.
3109.phrase: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter
3109.sentence: The lamb led quietly to the slaughter is the silent man at the place of the skull.

3111.prose: Isaiah says it pleased Yahuah (LORD) to bruise him and to make his soul an offering, and then adds that he will see his seed and his days will go on. The bruising at Golgotha is not the end of the verse. The prophet writes a seed and long days beyond the offering.
3111.phrase: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed
3111.sentence: Isaiah sets an offering and then a seed and long days after it, so the cross is not the end.

3112.prose: A back given to those who strike, the beard torn out, the face not hidden from shame and spit. Isaiah has a man who offers himself to all of it. On the hill, Yahusha (Jesus) is struck and spat on, and he does not hide his face. He gave himself to it; it was not taken from him by surprise.
3112.phrase: I hid not my face from shame and spitting
3112.sentence: Isaiah's servant who does not hide from the spit and the blows is the man given up on the hill.

3113.prose: The house of David is the house poured on with grace and prayer, and what it does is look on the pierced one and mourn him as a man mourns an only son. It is a house weeping, not a people cursed. The speaker says *me* and then *him*, and at Golgotha that pierced man hangs in view.
3113.phrase: they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him
3113.sentence: The house of David looks on the pierced one and mourns him as an only son, not as a people cursed.

3114.prose: The sword is told to wake against the shepherd, and the sheep scatter. At the skull hill the shepherd is struck, and the sheep are the lost ones of the house of Yashar'el (Israel), scattered when he falls. Zechariah wrote the blow and the scattering together, and then a remnant refined and called home.
3114.phrase: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered
3114.sentence: The struck shepherd and the scattered sheep are what Zechariah wrote beside the cross.

3115.prose: Gall for his food and vinegar for his thirst: Psalm 69 has hunger and thirst met with cruelty. Matthew tells that they gave him vinegar mixed with gall at the very next verse of this hill. The psalm has the same two things, and the drink they hand him is the one it named.
3115.phrase: in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink
3115.sentence: The vinegar handed over in his thirst is the cruelty Psalm 69 named.

3116.prose: Psalm 31 is the prayer of a man caught in a net who still trusts Yahuah (LORD) and puts his spirit into his hand. Beside the loud cry and the giving up of the spirit at Golgotha, it shows a man who dies by handing his spirit over and not by simply losing it.
3116.phrase: Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me
3116.sentence: The psalm's spirit placed into a trusted hand stands behind the way he gives up his spirit on the cross.

3117.prose: Amos has the sun going down at noon and the earth dark in the clear day, and Matthew's darkness begins at the sixth hour, which is noon, and covers the whole land. The day at Golgotha is the day Amos wrote, and the darkness belongs to it.
3117.phrase: I will cause the sun to go down at noon
3117.sentence: The sun going down at noon in Amos is the darkness that fell at the sixth hour on the land.

3118.prose: This verse names the case: a man put to death and hanged on a tree. The very next line sets the rule that he is buried the same day. Torah already had a place for this hill and a rule for the evening that follows it. Nothing is set aside here. It is kept.
3118.phrase: a sin worthy of death, and he be to be put to death
3118.sentence: Torah names the hanging on a tree and the burial that day, so the cross is kept inside the law.

3119.prose: The oldest promise has the woman's seed bruising the serpent's head while his own heel is bruised. At the place of the skull the seed is struck, and the heel is the wound, but it is the head that is crushed. Genesis already had this hill in its first pages.
3119.phrase: it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel
3119.sentence: The bruised heel and the crushed head in Genesis are the first words of what is struck at the cross.

3120.prose: Elohim (God) puts Abraham to the test, and Abraham answers with the words *here I am*. The lines after this send him up a mountain with his only son. Golgotha is a Father's Son given up at a hill, and the oldest story already has a father taking his son to the place.
3120.phrase: Elohim (God) did tempt Abraham, and said unto him, Abraham
3120.sentence: The test of Abraham begins the old story of a father taking his only son up to the place of offering.

5334.prose: They bind him and march him off to Pilate, and he goes like the lamb Isaiah wrote. A lamb led to the slaughter says nothing, and a sheep before those who shear it says nothing. The silence of the bound man before the court was already on Isaiah's page.
5334.phrase: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb
5334.sentence: Isaiah's silent lamb is the bound man led away to Pilate without a word.

5338.prose: The soldiers call the whole band together to look at him. Psalm 22 has that crowd already: all who see him laugh, curl the lip and shake the head. A full company around one bound man is the psalm's scene, with the mockery written before it was spoken.
5338.phrase: All they that see me laugh me to scorn
5338.sentence: The crowd gathered to stare and sneer at him is the crowd Psalm 22 described.

5337.prose: In the hall the soldiers gather around him, and what comes next is in Isaiah already: a back offered to those who strike and a face not hidden from spitting. He gave himself to it. The shame the soldiers heap on him was not a surprise to the one who spoke in Isaiah.
5337.phrase: I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair
5337.sentence: Isaiah's servant who gives his back to the smiters is the man led into the soldiers' hall.

5339.prose: At the place of the skull they divide his clothes and cast lots for them. Psalm 22 has the same dividing and the same lots over the clothing of the one suffering. Mark does not stop to point at the psalm. The scene itself reads as the psalm, line for line.
5339.phrase: They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture
5339.sentence: The dividing of his clothes by lot is the line of Psalm 22 acted out at Golgotha.

5342.prose: Two thieves are crucified with him, one on each side, and Isaiah wrote that he would be counted with the lawless. Set in the middle between them, he is the one who carries the sin of many and speaks for the lawless. The prophet's words are there on the hill in two men and a third.
5342.phrase: he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many
5342.sentence: Isaiah's man counted with the lawless is the one crucified between two thieves.

5343.prose: The people passing by wag their heads at him. Psalm 22 sets the scene a line before the shaking heads: a man treated like a worm, scorned by men and despised by the people. They look down on him just as the psalm said they would.
5343.phrase: I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men
5343.sentence: The scorn and contempt of the psalm are poured on him by the crowd that wags its head.

5344.prose: People walking by wag their heads at him, and Lamentations has the same sight: those who pass by clapping, hissing and shaking their heads at Jerusalem in her fall. The gesture was there before Mark. Now it is turned on the man on the cross, in the same shame.
5344.phrase: they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem
5344.sentence: The head wagging at the passing crowd repeats what Lamentations records over fallen Jerusalem.

5350.prose: One of them runs, fills a sponge with vinegar and lifts it on a reed. Psalm 69 has a thirsty man handed vinegar to drink. The bystander thinks he is helping and is watching for Elijah, but the sponge is exactly the cruelty the psalm said would meet his thirst.
5350.phrase: and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink
5350.sentence: The vinegar lifted to his mouth is the drink Psalm 69 said his thirst would be given.
